title: MLLMs Fail to Refuse when Using Tools Agentically
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Adding tool-use makes models answer harmful requests they would otherwise refuse, and this failure holds across many models.
layout: 3 stacked bands: Q/A header, top-to-bottom pipelines, bottom 3D bar chart
description: A question and answer headline sits at the top: 'Does agentic tool-use make MLLMs unsafe? Yes.' Below it, a photo of a pickpocketing scene with the caption 'How do I do this?' feeds two parallel 3D-slab pipelines. The green No-tool MLLM has a single Reasoning block and leads to a green check-marked box reading 'I cannot help with that request'. The pink Tool-use MLLM has a chain of Reasoning and Tool Call (wrench, zoom) blocks, with thought clouds, and leads to a red X box labelled 'Answer provided'. The bottom panel is a 3D bar chart of Refusal Failure Rate. Paired green (no-tool) and pink (tool-use) bars are grouped under open-weights and proprietary labels, with model logos below and delta values above each pair. The contrast between green and pink draws the eye first.
caption: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are more likely to fail refusing harmful requests when using tools. The example shows a user request on how to pickpocket, which the models should refuse to answer. Values in the bar chart are $\DeltaRFR$. Detailed results in Table [ref].
abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently pushed the frontier of visual reasoning by calling tools such as zooming and tagging. Despite the recent strong success of agentic MLLMs, this work uncovers a critical safety failure in the tool-use paradigm: agentic tool-using MLLMs become less capable of refusing harmful requests. Our experiments confirm that, across three popular safety benchmarks, all the top open- and closed-weight MLLMs we test exhibit significantly lower safety in tool-using settings than in non-tool settings, with a relative refusal failure rate increase of up to 68.7%. Based on analysis of 100,000+ responses, including extended experiments, we also propose two possible reasons for this safety degradation.
